name: Research Library
description: The Research Library is the evidence behind the HeadWater chronic stress survey and the Nebraska Stress Atlas. It exists so that a county, a hospital, a clinic or a health department writing a grant can cite the science in one click, and so that anyone can check what HeadWater measures against the studies that have held up. Each category matches a section of the survey or a layer of the Atlas. Each entry names who did the work, what they found, how many people were studied, and links to the publisher's record, the PubMed record and the free full text where one exists.
standard: A finding is included when it has been replicated in at least two independent populations, or comes from a meta-analysis or a cohort of tens of thousands, and has held for at least ten years. Federal surveillance data (BRFSS, Census, vital statistics) is included as the source for a measure itself.
Primary sources only: the original study or the federal record, never a news story or a vendor summary. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses rank above single studies.

Every entry carries a DOI or PubMed ID, the sample size, the population, one plain sentence on what it shows, and the date it was last checked. If the one sentence cannot be written from the record, the entry is not included.
Entries report what was measured. They do not report why. Where the study's own authors say an effect is small, the entry says so.

The bar is set by the evidence on the evidence: Ioannidis (2005) on why most published findings are false, and the 2015 Reproducibility Project, which replicated 36 of 100 psychology findings. Both are in the Methods shelf.
Nothing is added to pad a category. A category with two entries that have stood for twenty years is complete.

review.cadence: Once a year, and whenever a source is added or retired

cite_headwater.survey: Verdant Equanim, LLC. (2026). HeadWater chronic stress survey, version 2 (Nebraska Under Stress: Community Wellbeing Survey, Wave 2). Lincoln, Nebraska. https://verdantequanim.com
cite_headwater.atlas: Verdant Equanim, LLC. (2026). Nebraska Stress Atlas: county estimates from CDC PLACES and County Health Rankings with HeadWater survey layers. Lincoln, Nebraska. https://verdantequanim.com/atlas/ (data vintages shown on the page)
cite_headwater.reliability: Reliability of HeadWater version 1 subscales, March 2026 staff test (n = 86): Stability .79 (n = 64), Support .77 (n = 53), Sleep .65 (n = 52). Reported by subscale; rural validation is in progress.

categories.name: Chronic stress and chronic disease
categories.about: The spine of the platform: the physiology of long-running stress and the cohort evidence tying it to heart disease and early death. The honest reading of this shelf is that adult stress on its own is a modest risk factor, far smaller than smoking, and matters most as a trigger in people who already have disease, while stress in childhood and the social and economic conditions behind stress carry more weight. That is why HeadWater asks about early life, money, sleep and the people around you rather than only 'are you stressed'.

categories.name: Money, work and health
categories.about: Income, job security and job strain and their measured relationship to length and quality of life. The gradient runs through the whole income range, not only at the poverty line.

categories.name: Sleep
categories.survey: Stress & Sleep section; CDC PLACES short sleep; County Health Rankings insufficient sleep
categories.about: Three independent meta-analyses, covering more than five million people, give the same answer on short sleep and death, diabetes and obesity.

categories.name: Mood and anxiety
categories.survey: Feelings section; CDC PLACES frequent mental distress and depression
categories.about: Where HeadWater's mood items come from and how well two-item screens perform. This shelf documents the instruments more than the disease.

categories.name: Social connection and loneliness
categories.survey: People Around You section; CDC PLACES social and emotional support, loneliness
categories.about: Two meta-analyses from the same group a decade apart, covering more than 300,000 people, put the effect of social connection on survival in the same range as established medical risk factors.

categories.name: Childhood adversity
categories.about: Two entries, both unassailable: the original 1998 ACE study and the 2017 meta-analysis of 37 studies that confirmed its shape.

categories.name: Family history: famine, war and displacement
categories.about: Evidence developing. The Dutch Hunger Winter cohort is the one solid anchor: prenatal famine is consistently tied to adult body size, diabetes and schizophrenia; other outcomes are less robust and the proposed epigenetic mechanism is not settled. This shelf stays small on purpose.

categories.name: Food security and diet
categories.survey: Food section; CDC PLACES food insecurity; County Health Rankings food measures
categories.about: Food insecurity and clinical disease, and the burden of poor diet. The diabetes link is weaker than often claimed and the entries say so.

categories.name: Physical activity
categories.survey: Health & Environment section; CDC PLACES and County Health Rankings inactivity
categories.about: The burden of inactivity, estimated conservatively.

categories.name: Environment
categories.survey: Health & Environment section; County Health Rankings air and water measures
categories.about: Fine particulate air pollution and death, including below current national standards.

categories.name: Substance use
categories.survey: Substance Use section; CDC PLACES smoking; County Health Rankings smoking and excessive drinking
categories.about: Tobacco and alcohol burden from federal and global sources, and the source of HeadWater's drinking item.

categories.name: Access to help
categories.survey: Community Needs section; County Health Rankings provider rates and uninsured
categories.about: How much mental health need goes untreated, and the standard model of what determines whether people get care.

categories.name: Differences by race, sex, income and disability
categories.survey: About You section; County Health Rankings income and demographic measures
categories.about: Measured differences only, from federal vital statistics and large cohorts. Entries report the difference and the population it was measured in. They do not report why; that is for the reader, the county and the board.

categories.name: Methods and data sources
categories.about: How the public numbers on the Atlas are made, how HeadWater's reliability is reported, and the two papers that set this library's bar.

entries.source: Rockefeller University (McEwen)
entries.type: Review, New England Journal of Medicine
entries.title: Protective and damaging effects of stress mediators
entries.journal: The New England journal of medicine
entries.finding: Sets out allostatic load: the stress hormones that protect the body in the short run damage it when activation is sustained. The physiological frame behind the whole platform.
entries.citation: McEwen BS (1998). Protective and damaging effects of stress mediators. The New England journal of medicine. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199801153380307

entries.source: University of Montreal and Rockefeller University (Juster, McEwen, Lupien)
entries.title: Allostatic load biomarkers of chronic stress and impact on health and cognition
entries.finding: Indexes combining neuroendocrine, immune, metabolic and cardiovascular markers predict illness and death beyond what standard clinical measures predict.
entries.citation: Juster RP et al. (2010). Allostatic load biomarkers of chronic stress and impact on health and cognition. Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2009.10.002

entries.source: Carnegie Mellon University (Cohen)
entries.title: Psychological stress and disease
entries.finding: Summarizes the evidence that chronic stress contributes to depression, cardiovascular disease and the course of HIV and cancer, through both behavior and biology. Short and widely cited; a starting point, not a data paper.
entries.citation: Cohen S et al. (2007). Psychological stress and disease. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.298.14.1685

entries.source: University College London (Steptoe, Kivimäki)
entries.title: Stress and cardiovascular disease
entries.finding: Chronic stress predicts first coronary events; work stress, social isolation and loneliness each raise the risk; acute stress triggers events in people with advanced atherosclerosis.
entries.citation: Steptoe A and Kivimäki M (2012). Stress and cardiovascular disease. Nature reviews. Cardiology. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrcardio.2012.45

entries.source: University College London (Kivimäki, Steptoe)
entries.title: Effects of stress on the development and progression of cardiovascular disease
entries.finding: Severe childhood stress raises the risk of multiple adult chronic conditions. Adult stress effects are, in the authors' words, generally less marked than childhood stress and classic risk factors such as smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol; adult stress matters most as a trigger in people with existing plaque and as a determinant of outcome in those with existing disease.
entries.citation: Kivimäki M and Steptoe A (2018). Effects of stress on the development and progression of cardiovascular disease. Nature reviews. Cardiology. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrcardio.2017.189

entries.source: Stanford, MIT and Harvard (Chetty, Cutler and colleagues) with the US Treasury
entries.title: The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014
entries.sample: 1.4 billion person-years from tax records, 2001 to 2014
entries.finding: Men in the top 1 percent of income lived 14.6 years longer than men in the bottom 1 percent; women, 10.1 years. The gap widened over the period. Among low-income people, life expectancy varied by about 4.5 years across local areas, and that variation tracked smoking and other health behaviors, not access to medical care, income inequality or local labor markets.
entries.citation: Chetty R et al. (2016). The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.4226

entries.source: University College London (Marmot)
entries.title: Health inequalities among British civil servants: the Whitehall II study
entries.finding: Twenty years after the first Whitehall study, lower employment grade still meant more angina, more ECG evidence of ischemia, more chronic bronchitis, worse self-rated health, more smoking, less exercise, less job control and less social support. The gradient ran through every grade, not only the bottom.
entries.citation: Marmot MG et al. (1991). Health inequalities among British civil servants: the Whitehall II study. Lancet (London, England). https://doi.org/10.1016/0140-6736(91)93068-k

entries.source: University of California San Francisco and colleagues (Adler)
entries.title: Socioeconomic status and health. The challenge of the gradient
entries.finding: Socioeconomic status is associated with health at every level, not only below the poverty line, which means the mechanisms have to work across the whole range.
entries.citation: Adler NE et al. (1994). Socioeconomic status and health. The challenge of the gradient. The American psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037//0003-066x.49.1.15

entries.source: IPD-Work Consortium, University College London (Kivimäki)
entries.title: Job strain as a risk factor for coronary heart disease: a collaborative meta-analysis of individual participant data
entries.sample: 197,473 employees in 13 European cohorts; 2,358 coronary events
entries.population: Working adults without heart disease at baseline
entries.finding: Job strain raised the risk of a first coronary event by 23 percent after adjustment, with a population attributable risk of 3.4 percent. The authors state the effect is much smaller than standard risk factors such as smoking.
entries.citation: Kivimäki M et al. (2012). Job strain as a risk factor for coronary heart disease: a collaborative meta-analysis of individual participant data. Lancet (London, England). https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(12)60994-5

entries.source: University of Warwick (Cappuccio)
entries.title: Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies
entries.finding: Short sleep raised the risk of death by 12 percent; long sleep by 30 percent. No publication bias found.
entries.citation: Cappuccio FP et al. (2010). Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/33.5.585

entries.source: Oita University, Nihon University and Kyoto University (Itani, Kaneita)
entries.title: Short sleep duration and health outcomes: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
entries.population: Adults, follow-up one year or more
entries.finding: Short sleep raised mortality 12 percent, diabetes 37 percent, hypertension 17 percent, cardiovascular disease 16 percent, coronary heart disease 26 percent and obesity 38 percent. Mortality rose in a straight line below six hours.
entries.citation: Itani O et al. (2017). Short sleep duration and health outcomes: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression. Sleep medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sleep.2016.08.006

entries.source: University of Warwick (Cappuccio)
entries.title: Quantity and quality of sleep and incidence of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
entries.finding: Short sleep raised new type 2 diabetes 28 percent; trouble falling asleep, 57 percent; trouble staying asleep, 84 percent. Quality of sleep predicted diabetes as strongly as quantity.
entries.citation: Cappuccio FP et al. (2010). Quantity and quality of sleep and incidence of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Diabetes care. https://doi.org/10.2337/dc09-1124

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: About Sleep
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.finding: Defines the adult recommendation of seven or more hours and the short-sleep measure used in PLACES.
entries.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Sleep. https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html

entries.source: Indiana University and Columbia University (Kroenke, Spitzer, Williams)
entries.title: The Patient Health Questionnaire-2: validity of a two-item depression screener
entries.sample: 6,000 patients in 15 clinics; 580 interviewed by a mental health professional
entries.finding: The two-item PHQ-2 (depressed mood and loss of interest over two weeks) at a score of 3 or more detected major depression with 83 percent sensitivity and 92 percent specificity. HeadWater's interest and mood items follow this form.
entries.citation: Kroenke K et al. (2003). The Patient Health Questionnaire-2: validity of a two-item depression screener. Medical care. https://doi.org/10.1097/01.MLR.0000093487.78664.3C

entries.source: Indiana University and Columbia University (Kroenke, Spitzer, Williams)
entries.type: Instrument validation, Annals of Internal Medicine
entries.title: Anxiety disorders in primary care: prevalence, impairment, comorbidity, and detection
entries.sample: 965 patients in 15 US primary care clinics
entries.finding: One in five patients had an anxiety disorder; 41 percent of them were receiving no treatment. The two core GAD items (nervous or on edge; unable to stop worrying) screened well for all four anxiety disorders studied. HeadWater's anxiety item follows this form.
entries.citation: Kroenke K et al. (2007). Anxiety disorders in primary care: prevalence, impairment, comorbidity, and detection. Annals of internal medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-146-5-200703060-00004

entries.source: Carnegie Mellon University and University of Oregon (Cohen, Kamarck, Mermelstein)
entries.type: Instrument, Journal of Health and Social Behavior
entries.title: A global measure of perceived stress
entries.journal: Journal of health and social behavior
entries.finding: The Perceived Stress Scale, the most used measure of how uncontrollable and overloaded people find their lives. HeadWater's stress, overwhelm and control items are in its family.
entries.citation: Cohen S et al. (1983). A global measure of perceived stress. Journal of health and social behavior. PMID 6668417.

entries.source: Brigham Young University (Holt-Lunstad, Smith, Layton)
entries.title: Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review
entries.population: Adults, all ages and health states
entries.finding: People with stronger social relationships had 50 percent higher odds of survival over the follow-up period, consistent across age, sex, initial health and cause of death. The effect was strongest for measures of social integration and weakest for simply living with others.
entries.citation: Holt-Lunstad J et al. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS medicine. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316

entries.source: Brigham Young University (Holt-Lunstad and colleagues)
entries.title: Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review
entries.finding: After controlling for confounders, social isolation raised the likelihood of death 29 percent, loneliness 26 percent and living alone 32 percent. Effects were larger in samples under age 65.
entries.citation: Holt-Lunstad J et al. (2015). Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. Perspectives on psychological science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691614568352

entries.source: St. Luke's and Mount Sinai, New York (Cohen, Bavishi, Rozanski)
entries.title: Purpose in Life and Its Relationship to All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Meta-Analysis
entries.finding: A higher sense of purpose in life was associated with 17 percent lower all-cause mortality and 17 percent fewer cardiovascular events, consistent across countries, questionnaires and age. Source for HeadWater's meaning item.
entries.citation: Cohen R et al. (2016). Purpose in Life and Its Relationship to All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Meta-Analysis. Psychosomatic medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/PSY.0000000000000274

entries.source: Kaiser Permanente and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Felitti, Anda)
entries.type: Cohort, American Journal of Preventive Medicine
entries.title: Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults. The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study
entries.sample: 9,508 adults (70.5 percent response) at a large HMO
entries.finding: Compared with none, four or more categories of childhood abuse or household dysfunction meant 4 to 12 times the risk of alcoholism, drug abuse, depression and suicide attempt; 2 to 4 times the risk of smoking and poor self-rated health; and a graded rise in heart disease, cancer, lung disease, fractures and liver disease. Source of HeadWater's childhood experiences item.
entries.citation: Felitti VJ et al. (1998). Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults. The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study. American journal of preventive medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0749-3797(98)00017-8

entries.source: Public Health Wales and Liverpool John Moores University (Hughes, Bellis) with the World Health Organization
entries.title: The effect of multiple adverse childhood experiences on health: a systematic review and meta-analysis
entries.finding: Four or more ACEs raised every health outcome studied: weak to modest for inactivity, obesity and diabetes; moderate for smoking, heavy drinking, cancer, heart disease and respiratory disease; strong for mental illness and problem drinking; strongest, over sevenfold, for problem drug use and interpersonal and self-directed violence.
entries.citation: Hughes K et al. (2017). The effect of multiple adverse childhood experiences on health: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet. Public health. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(17)30118-4

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: About Adverse Childhood Experiences
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.finding: CDC's definition of ACEs and the national prevalence figures from BRFSS.
entries.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Adverse Childhood Experiences. https://www.cdc.gov/aces/about/index.html

entries.source: University of Amsterdam (Roseboom)
entries.title: The Dutch famine and its long-term consequences for adult health
entries.sample: 2,414 people born around the Dutch famine of 1944 to 1945
entries.finding: Famine exposure in the womb was associated with glucose intolerance at every stage of gestation; early-gestation exposure with more coronary heart disease, worse lipids, disturbed clotting, higher stress responsiveness, more obesity and, in women, more breast cancer. Effects depended on timing.
entries.citation: Roseboom T et al. (2006). The Dutch famine and its long-term consequences for adult health. Early human development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.earlhumdev.2006.07.001

entries.source: Columbia University and Emory University (Lumey, Stein, Susser)
entries.type: Review, Annual Review of Public Health
entries.title: Prenatal famine and adult health
entries.population: Adults exposed to famine before birth
entries.finding: Across famine studies, prenatal famine is consistently tied to adult body size, diabetes and schizophrenia. For other outcomes the findings are less robust, and the epigenetic mechanism remains a hypothesis. This is why the shelf is labeled evidence developing.
entries.citation: Lumey LH et al. (2011). Prenatal famine and adult health. Annual review of public health. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-publhealth-031210-101230

entries.source: University of Illinois and University of Kentucky (Gundersen, Ziliak)
entries.title: Food Insecurity And Health Outcomes
entries.finding: Food insecurity is consistently associated with worse health after confounders are controlled: food-insecure children at least twice as likely to be in fair or poor health; food-insecure seniors with limitations comparable to food-secure seniors fourteen years older.
entries.citation: Gundersen C and Ziliak JP (2015). Food Insecurity And Health Outcomes. Health affairs. https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2015.0645

entries.source: University of California San Francisco (Seligman, Laraia, Kushel)
entries.title: Food insecurity is associated with chronic disease among low-income NHANES participants
entries.sample: 5,094 low-income adults aged 18 to 65, NHANES 1999 to 2004
entries.finding: Food insecurity was associated with 20 percent higher hypertension and 30 percent higher hyperlipidemia. The association with diabetes was not statistically significant except under a strict definition of food insecurity.
entries.citation: Seligman HK et al. (2010). Food insecurity is associated with chronic disease among low-income NHANES participants. The Journal of nutrition. https://doi.org/10.3945/jn.109.112573

entries.source: Global Burden of Disease Diet Collaborators, Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation
entries.title: Health effects of dietary risks in 195 countries, 1990-2017: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017
entries.finding: Eleven million deaths in 2017 were attributable to diet, led by high sodium, low whole grains and low fruit. Dietary data were uneven across countries and the authors flag the resulting uncertainty.
entries.citation: GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators (2019). Health effects of dietary risks in 195 countries, 1990-2017: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(19)30041-8

entries.source: Harvard Medical School and the Lancet Physical Activity Series Working Group (Lee, Blair)
entries.title: Effect of physical inactivity on major non-communicable diseases worldwide: an analysis of burden of disease and life expectancy
entries.finding: Using conservative assumptions, inactivity accounts for 6 percent of coronary heart disease, 7 percent of type 2 diabetes, 10 percent of breast and colon cancer and 9 percent of premature deaths, about 5.3 million deaths in 2008.
entries.citation: Lee IM et al. (2012). Effect of physical inactivity on major non-communicable diseases worldwide: an analysis of burden of disease and life expectancy. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(12)61031-9

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: Benefits of Physical Activity
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.finding: CDC's summary of the health benefits of physical activity and the adult guideline of 150 minutes a week of moderate activity.
entries.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Benefits of Physical Activity. https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/benefits/index.html

entries.source: Brigham Young University and Harvard School of Public Health (Pope, Dockery)
entries.type: Critical review, Journal of the Air and Waste Management Association
entries.title: Health effects of fine particulate air pollution: lines that connect
entries.journal: Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association
entries.finding: A comprehensive evaluation of six lines of research gives persuasive evidence that fine particulate air pollution harms cardiopulmonary health, at different time scales of exposure.
entries.citation: Pope CA 3rd and Dockery DW (2006). Health effects of fine particulate air pollution: lines that connect. Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association. https://doi.org/10.1080/10473289.2006.10464485

entries.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Di, Dominici, Schwartz)
entries.type: Cohort, New England Journal of Medicine
entries.title: Air Pollution and Mortality in the Medicare Population
entries.journal: The New England journal of medicine
entries.finding: Each 10 micrograms per cubic meter of fine particulate matter raised all-cause mortality 7.3 percent, and 13.6 percent when exposure was already below the national standard. Effects were larger for men, Black beneficiaries and people eligible for Medicaid.
entries.citation: Di Q et al. (2017). Air Pollution and Mortality in the Medicare Population. The New England journal of medicine. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1702747

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: Cigarette Smoking
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.finding: CDC's summary of smoking prevalence and the diseases it causes, drawing on the Surgeon General's reports.
entries.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cigarette Smoking. https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/about/index.html

entries.source: Global Burden of Disease Alcohol Collaborators, Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation
entries.title: Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990-2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016
entries.sample: 694 data sources and 592 studies; 195 countries, 1990 to 2016
entries.finding: Alcohol was the seventh leading risk factor for death in 2016 and the leading risk factor for ages 15 to 49. In this analysis the level of consumption that minimized health loss was zero drinks a week. Later analyses debate the low-dose estimate; the overall burden finding stands.
entries.citation: GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (2018). Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990-2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31310-2

entries.source: VA Puget Sound and University of Washington (Bush, Bradley)
entries.type: Instrument validation, Archives of Internal Medicine
entries.title: The AUDIT alcohol consumption questions (AUDIT-C): an effective brief screening test for problem drinking
entries.sample: 243 male veterans in three VA clinics
entries.finding: The three AUDIT-C consumption questions detected heavy drinking as well as the full ten-item AUDIT. Small and male-only; included as the source of HeadWater's drinking item, not as evidence about drinking.
entries.citation: Bush K et al. (1998). The AUDIT alcohol consumption questions (AUDIT-C): an effective brief screening test for problem drinking. Archives of internal medicine. https://doi.org/10.1001/archinte.158.16.1789

entries.source: Harvard Medical School (Kessler)
entries.type: Repeated national survey, New England Journal of Medicine
entries.title: Prevalence and treatment of mental disorders, 1990 to 2003
entries.journal: The New England journal of medicine
entries.sample: 5,388 interviews (1990 to 1992) and 4,319 (2001 to 2003), National Comorbidity Survey
entries.finding: About three in ten adults had a mental disorder in the past year in both decades. Treatment rose from 20 percent to 33 percent of those with a disorder, which means most people with a disorder still received no treatment.
entries.citation: Kessler RC et al. (2005). Prevalence and treatment of mental disorders, 1990 to 2003. The New England journal of medicine. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa043266

entries.source: University of California Los Angeles (Andersen)
entries.type: Model review, Journal of Health and Social Behavior
entries.title: Revisiting the behavioral model and access to medical care: does it matter?
entries.journal: Journal of health and social behavior
entries.finding: The Behavioral Model of Health Services Use: whether people get care depends on predisposing factors, enabling resources and need. The standard frame for HeadWater's community needs and confidence items.
entries.citation: Andersen RM (1995). Revisiting the behavioral model and access to medical care: does it matter? Journal of health and social behavior. PMID 7738325.

entries.source: National Center for Health Statistics (Murphy, Kochanek, Xu, Arias)
entries.title: Mortality in the United States, 2023 (NCHS Data Brief 521)
authors: National Center for Health Statistics (Murphy, Kochanek, Xu, Arias)
entries.finding: Life expectancy and age-adjusted death rates by race, ethnicity and sex for 2023, from the National Vital Statistics System. The current federal reference for differences in length of life.
entries.citation: Murphy SL, Kochanek KD, Xu J, Arias E. (2024). Mortality in the United States, 2023. NCHS Data Brief No. 521. National Center for Health Statistics. https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db521.htm

entries.source: National Center for Health Statistics (Kochanek, Arias, Anderson)
entries.type: Federal vital statistics, NCHS Data Brief
entries.title: How did cause of death contribute to racial differences in life expectancy in the United States in 2010?
entries.finding: In 2010 life expectancy for the Black population was 3.8 years lower than for the White population (4.7 years for males, 3.3 for females), accounted for by higher death rates from heart disease, cancer, homicide, diabetes, stroke and perinatal conditions. Kept for the cause-of-death breakdown; the 2023 brief carries the current figures.
entries.citation: Kochanek KD et al. (2013). How did cause of death contribute to racial differences in life expectancy in the United States in 2010? NCHS data brief. PMID 24152376.

entries.source: Stanford, MIT and Harvard (Chetty, Cutler and colleagues) with the US Treasury
entries.title: The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014
entries.finding: The income gap in life expectancy, 14.6 years for men and 10.1 for women between the top and bottom 1 percent, with local variation tied to health behaviors.
entries.citation: Chetty R et al. (2016). The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.4226

entries.source: National Institutes of Health and the Administration for Community Living (Krahn, Walker, Correa-De-Araujo)
entries.type: Review and position paper, American Journal of Public Health
entries.title: Persons with disabilities as an unrecognized health disparity population
entries.population: US adults with significant disabilities, more than 12 percent of the population
entries.finding: Summarizes documented differences in health outcomes for people with disabilities and argues they meet the criteria for a health disparity population. Included for the documented differences; the policy recommendations are the authors' own.
entries.citation: Krahn GL et al. (2015). Persons with disabilities as an unrecognized health disparity population. American journal of public health. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2014.302182

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: PLACES: Local Data for Better Health, methodology
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.sample: All US counties, places, tracts and ZIP code areas
entries.finding: How the CDC PLACES county estimates on the Atlas are made: small area estimation from BRFSS responses, Census population data and ACS characteristics. The estimates are modeled, not direct counts.
entries.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. PLACES: Local Data for Better Health, Methodology. https://www.cdc.gov/places/methodology/index.html

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: PLACES measure definitions
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.finding: The exact wording of each PLACES measure on the Atlas, including the BRFSS question behind it.
entries.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. PLACES Measure Definitions. https://www.cdc.gov/places/measure-definitions/index.html

entries.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.title: Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
entries.finding: The telephone survey behind both PLACES and the County Health Rankings behavior and health measures.

entries.source: University of Ioannina and Tufts (Ioannidis)
entries.title: Why most published research findings are false
entries.finding: A research finding is less likely to be true when studies are small, effects are small, many relationships are tested, designs are flexible and there is financial or other interest. The reason this library requires replication and size.
entries.citation: Ioannidis JP (2005). Why most published research findings are false. PLoS medicine. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124

entries.source: Open Science Collaboration (270 contributors)
entries.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
entries.sample: 100 published psychology studies replicated with high-powered designs
entries.finding: Thirty-six percent of replications were statistically significant versus 97 percent of the originals; replication effects were half the size. Replication success tracked the strength of the original evidence. The reason single studies do not make this library.
entries.citation: Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716
